candidate.answerReason: The allowed centers form the intersection lens of the two unit disks centered at A and B. Sweeping a unit disk over that lens adds two 120° annular sectors and two 60° unit sectors. Adding their areas to the lens area gives 3π-√3/2.

methods.label: Find the allowed centers and the swept boundary
methods.explanation:
A radius-\(1\) disk centered at \(O\) covers \(\overline{AB}\) exactly when \(OA\le1\) and \(OB\le1\). These inequalities are necessary because the endpoints must be covered. They are sufficient because a disk contains the entire segment joining any two of its points. Thus the allowed centers fill the lens \(L\) formed by intersecting the unit disks centered at \(A\) and \(B\).

Let \(U\) and \(V\) be the two intersections of their boundary circles. The triangles \(ABU\) and \(ABV\) are equilateral with side \(1\). Their altitudes have length
\[
\sqrt{1-\left(\frac12\right)^2}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2},
\]
so \(UV=\sqrt3\). Each boundary arc of \(L\) subtends \(120^\circ\) at its center. Each of the two circular segments making up \(L\) is therefore a \(120^\circ\) unit sector minus a triangle with base \(UV\) and height \(\tfrac12\). Hence
\[
\operatorname{area}(L)
=2\left(\frac{\pi}{3}-\frac12\cdot\sqrt3\cdot\frac12\right)
=\frac{2\pi}{3}-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}.
\]
We next determine how the disks extend beyond this lens. A supporting line touches a region and leaves it entirely on one side. Take a supporting line of \(L\) touching it at \(O\), and shift the line outward by \(1\). Every allowed center lies behind the original line, so every radius-\(1\) disk lies behind the shifted line. The disk centered at \(O\) touches that shifted line.

Both \(L\) and its disk sweep are convex, meaning that they contain segments joining their points. For the sweep, take the same fractional step between two covered points and between their allowed centers. The new center stays in \(L\), and the triangle inequality keeps the new point within distance \(1\) of that center. Consequently, the shifted supporting lines in all directions determine the entire outside boundary of \(S\).

Along either \(120^\circ\) arc of \(L\), shifting outward extends its radii from \(1\) to \(2\). This adds an annular sector of angle \(120^\circ\). At each corner \(U\) or \(V\), the outward radius directions from \(A\) and \(B\) differ by \(60^\circ\). The connecting outside boundary is therefore a radius-\(1\) arc centered at that corner, adding a \(60^\circ\) sector.

The two \(120^\circ\) direction ranges and two \(60^\circ\) ranges exhaust a full turn. The rays continuing \(AU,BU,AV,BV\) beyond the corners separate adjacent added pieces, so their interiors do not overlap. Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{area}(S)
&=\operatorname{area}(L)
+2\cdot\frac{120}{360}\pi(2^2-1^2)
+2\cdot\frac{60}{360}\pi\\
&=\frac{2\pi}{3}-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}
+2\pi+\frac{\pi}{3}\\
&=\boxed{3\pi-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The answer is \(\text{C}\).
